note: Checked live doc 01 and Wayback doc 02. Both contain the CSIS interactive repository description and define its LEO cost-per-kilogram metric, but neither supplies the vehicle-level chart data or a Space Shuttle value; searches for Shuttle and 54,500 found only a bibliography reference to a Shuttle cost paper, not the claimed figure. The about-$54,500/kg claim therefore cannot be verified from these documents.

Checked TechCrunch live doc 01 and Wayback docs 02–03. They say W-1 came home in February 2024 and identify its landing as the first commercial spacecraft landing on a military test range and the first on U.S. soil under FAA Part 450. They also say the first commercial land reentry ever attempted was the effort before W-1's landing. Revised the broad ‘first commercial land reentry in the United States’ wording to the specifically supported Part 450/U.S.-soil description; dropped the unsupported broad superlative.

The originally cited NASA URL returned 404 (doc 01), so I fetched NASA's own replacement release, live doc 02 and Wayback doc 03; both contain the same substantive text. NASA dates the release July 17, 2024 and says it announced an intent to discontinue VIPER development because of cost increases, launch delays and future-cost-growth risks. It does not state the claimed approximately $450M already spent, so that figure is dropped; ‘intent to discontinue development’ preserves NASA's precise description.

The original China-in-Space URL returned 404 and had no Wayback captures. I fetched the CNSA publication (live doc 02; Wayback doc 03), which directly calls the facility the ILRS and states it is projected in two phases, with ‘a basic model to be built by 2035 in the lunar south pole region.’ Corrected ‘basic lunar base’ to the source's term ‘basic model’; the source supports the target region and year.

Checked SpaceNews live doc 01. It has substantive headline/summary text specifying Cosmic Shielding, the $4 million TACFI contract, AFRL, and the tool's purpose; the article body is behind a registration/subscription wall. The document does not substantiate the legacy claim's ‘nanocomposite’ characterization or that seven systems are now in space, so both are dropped. Checked Wikipedia live doc 01 and Wayback doc 02. Both state the starting price for delivering payloads to orbit is about US$7.5 million per launch or US$25,000 per kg; neither gives $19,039/kg. Corrected the amount to the source's per-kilogram price and retained its explicit metric scope.

Checked live doc 01 and Wayback doc 02. Because this is substantive text about the experiment but does not establish the claimed later production result, no alternative source was sought.

Checked live doc 01 (the URL resolves to SpaceNews’ “NASA Budget Betrays Vision for Space Exploration”). The original cited Redwire URL is dead (doc 1, HTTP 404; no captures). As permitted for a dead original, fetched Redwire’s own press release (doc 2). NASA's live article (doc 01; doc 02 is a substantively matching capture) says pure molecular oxygen was measured during vacuum-chamber testing on simulated lunar soil and attributes a first to NASA producing molecular oxygen using this process. Its caption dates the pictured testing to Dec. 5, 2024, while the article is dated May 5, 2025; it does not establish that the testing occurred in May 2025 or that it was the first such production overall. The corrected sentence drops those overstatements and states only the documented result and method.

The original Space Forge URL produced only 10 characters (doc 01), so I checked the company's primary press release (alt-live doc 02; doc 03 is its Wayback capture). The press release dates ForgeStar-1's launch June 27, 2025, and explicitly says “While ForgeStar-1 won’t return to Earth”; it describes return as a capability for future missions. This contradicts the claimed May 2025 completed payload return. Review: downgraded from refuted: the cited (dead) URL is a release about a returned second payload; ForgeStar-1 not returning does not contradict the return of a different payload.

NBC's live article (doc 01; doc 02 is a matching Wayback capture) records the event update on May 27, 2025, identifies Flight 9 as the first reuse of a previously flown Super Heavy booster, and reports that the booster exploded shortly before splashdown. These passages substantiate the date, first-reuse qualifier, and booster loss in the claim.
